title: Gradient direction — the angle that orients every edge
description: Sobel gives two numbers per pixel; their ratio is the gradient angle. Learn how θ = atan2(Gy, Gx) orients each edge and why Canny folds it into four bins.

sections.title: The gradient has a direction, not just a size

data.markdown:
## The gradient has a direction, not just a size

In the Sobel lesson we kept the gradient **magnitude** — one number per pixel saying *how fast* the image changes. But the Sobel step actually hands us **two** numbers per pixel: $G_x$ (change left-to-right) and $G_y$ (change top-to-bottom). Together they form a little arrow, the gradient vector $\nabla I = (G_x,\, G_y)$.

![Diagram of a slanted boundary between a dark region and a bright region. A red arrow labelled grad I points from the dark side toward the bright side, perpendicular to the boundary; a green dashed arrow lies along the boundary; the angle theta between the gradient arrow and the horizontal axis is marked.](/api/courses/edge-detection-basics/assets/images/gradient-direction-diagram.png)

That arrow has a **direction**, and the direction carries real information: the gradient always points *across* the edge, from the dark side toward the bright side — never along it. So the edge itself runs **perpendicular** to the gradient.

We read the angle off the two components with the two-argument arctangent:

$$ \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(G_y,\, G_x) $$

- $\theta$ ("theta") is the angle of the arrow, measured anticlockwise from the $+x$ axis.
- $\operatorname{atan2}(y, x)$ is $\arctan(y/x)$ that *also* inspects the **signs** of $y$ and $x$, so it returns the correct angle in all four quadrants — range $(-180^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}]$ — instead of collapsing opposite directions onto each other.

Because an edge and its $180^{\circ}$ flip trace the *same* line, we usually fold $\theta$ into $[0^{\circ}, 180^{\circ})$: it is an **orientation**, not a signed heading. That single angle is exactly what the next stage of Canny consumes.

sections.title: Check: which way does the gradient point?
sections.description: Pin down the relationship between the gradient vector and the edge before moving on.

data.question: At a clean boundary between a dark region and a bright region, which way does the gradient vector ∇I point?
options: Across the edge — perpendicular to it, from the dark side toward the bright side
Along the edge — parallel to the boundary line
Straight up the +y axis, no matter how the edge is oriented
Across the edge, but from the bright side toward the dark side
data.explanation: The gradient points in the direction of fastest intensity increase, so at a dark→bright boundary it points straight across the edge toward the higher values — dark to bright. The edge line itself is therefore perpendicular to ∇I. 'Along the edge' confuses the edge's tangent with the gradient; the +y answer ignores that the angle depends on the edge's orientation; and the last option has the right axis but the wrong sign — intensity rises toward the bright side, so the arrow points dark→bright.

sections.title: From a continuous angle to four bins

data.markdown:
## From a continuous angle to four bins

Canny's next step — **non-maximum suppression (NMS)** — thins the fuzzy gradient ridge down to a one-pixel-wide line. To do that it asks, at every pixel: *is this pixel a local maximum of the gradient magnitude along the gradient direction?* If a neighbour across the edge has a stronger gradient, this pixel is not the true crest and gets suppressed.

Comparing along an arbitrary real-valued angle would mean **interpolating** between pixels. Canny sidesteps that by **snapping** each angle to one of four directions that line up with the pixel grid and its diagonals:

![Compass diagram with four coloured spokes through the origin labelled 0 degrees (horizontal), 45 degrees, 90 degrees (vertical) and 135 degrees; each spoke is a full line because an orientation and its 180-degree flip are the same direction.](/api/courses/edge-detection-basics/assets/images/nms-direction-bins.png)

| Folded angle $\theta$ | Bin | Neighbours compared |
|---|---|---|
| $[0^{\circ}, 22.5^{\circ}) \cup [157.5^{\circ}, 180^{\circ})$ | **0°** | left & right |
| $[22.5^{\circ}, 67.5^{\circ})$ | **45°** | the two ↗↙ diagonals |
| $[67.5^{\circ}, 112.5^{\circ})$ | **90°** | up & down |
| $[112.5^{\circ}, 157.5^{\circ})$ | **135°** | the two ↖↘ diagonals |

With the angle bucketed, NMS just peeks at two **integer-offset** neighbours — no interpolation, no floating-point indexing. The plot below shows this folding as a step function.

sections.description: Trace any gradient angle up to the curve to read which of the four NMS bins it lands in.

data.alt: Step plot. The x-axis is the gradient angle from 0 to 180 degrees; the y-axis is the assigned non-maximum-suppression bin: 0, 45, 90 or 135 degrees. The curve sits at 0 degrees for angles below 22.5 and above 157.5, steps up to 45 between 22.5 and 67.5, to 90 between 67.5 and 112.5, and to 135 between 112.5 and 157.5. data.caption: Figure 1 — Each continuous gradient angle is folded into one of four discrete NMS directions. The bin boundaries sit at the half-angles 22.5°, 67.5°, 112.5° and 157.5°.
data.sourceCode:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Canny folds each gradient angle (0..180 deg) into one of four
# discrete directions before non-maximum suppression. This plot shows
# that mapping as a step function: read an angle off the x-axis, follow
# it up to the curve, and the y-value is the bin its edge is tested in.
angles = np.linspace(0, 180, 1000)


def to_bin(a):
    a = a % 180
    if a < 22.5 or a >= 157.5:
        return 0
    if a < 67.5:
        return 45
    if a < 112.5:
        return 90
    return 135


bins = np.array([to_bin(a) for a in angles])

plt.figure(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))
plt.step(angles, bins, where="mid", lw=2.2, color="#d1495b")
for edge in (22.5, 67.5, 112.5, 157.5):
    plt.axvline(edge, color="#888", ls=":", lw=1.0)
plt.yticks([0, 45, 90, 135], ["0° (→)", "45° (↗)", "90° (↑)", "135° (↖)"])
plt.xticks(np.arange(0, 181, 22.5))
plt.xlabel("Gradient angle from arctan2(gy, gx)  [degrees]")
plt.ylabel("Assigned NMS direction bin")
plt.title("Folding a continuous gradient angle into 4 NMS bins")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.savefig(
    "courses/edge-detection-basics/assets/plots/gradient-direction-1.png",
    dpi=110,
    bbox_inches="tight",
)

sections.title: Compute the gradient direction
sections.description: Turn the two Sobel derivatives into a per-pixel angle, then watch the orientations light up as colour.

data.taskMarkdown:
Write `gradient_direction_deg(gray)` that returns the **per-pixel gradient direction in degrees**, folded into the range `[0, 180)`.

The recipe is three lines:

1. `gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)` and `gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)` — the two first derivatives.
2. `ang = np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(gy, gx))` — the signed angle in `(-180, 180]`.
3. `np.mod(ang, 180.0)` — fold opposite directions together so the result is an **orientation** in `[0, 180)`.

```
gradient_direction_deg(vertical_edge_image)  ->  ~0°   (gradient runs left↔right)
gradient_direction_deg(horizontal_edge_image) ->  ~90°  (gradient runs up↕down)
```

The visualisation below the editor is already written: it encodes your angle as **hue** and the gradient strength as **brightness**, so each edge orientation gets its own colour. Press ▶ Run and the static reference image is replaced by *your* output — match it.
data.starterCode:
import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def gradient_direction_deg(gray):
    """Per-pixel gradient direction in degrees, folded to [0, 180)."""
    # TODO:
    # 1. gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
    # 2. gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
    # 3. ang = np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(gy, gx))   # (-180, 180]
    # 4. return np.mod(ang, 180.0)              # fold to [0, 180)
    raise NotImplementedError("implement gradient_direction_deg")


# ---- visualisation (already written for you) ----
# The reference image on the left is mounted at /inputs/input-direction.png.
img = cv2.imread('/inputs/input-direction.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
theta_deg = gradient_direction_deg(img)

gx = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
gy = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
mag = np.sqrt(gx * gx + gy * gy)

# Hue = direction, Saturation = full, Value = gradient strength.
hsv = np.zeros((*img.shape, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
hsv[..., 0] = (theta_deg / 180.0 * 179).astype(np.uint8)   # OpenCV hue is 0..179
hsv[..., 1] = 255
hsv[..., 2] = (mag / mag.max() * 255).astype(np.uint8)
rgb = cv2.cvtColor(hsv, cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB)

plt.imshow(rgb)
plt.axis('off')

data.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def gradient_direction_deg(gray):
    gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
    gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
    ang = np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(gy, gx))   # (-180, 180]
    return np.mod(ang, 180.0)              # fold to [0, 180)


img = cv2.imread('/inputs/input-direction.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
theta_deg = gradient_direction_deg(img)

gx = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
gy = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
mag = np.sqrt(gx * gx + gy * gy)

hsv = np.zeros((*img.shape, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
hsv[..., 0] = (theta_deg / 180.0 * 179).astype(np.uint8)
hsv[..., 1] = 255
hsv[..., 2] = (mag / mag.max() * 255).astype(np.uint8)
rgb = cv2.cvtColor(hsv, cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB)

plt.imshow(rgb)
plt.axis('off')

data.starterCode:
import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Build your own scene and watch its edge orientations turn into colour.
# Try: rotate the rectangle, add a second line at a different angle,
# or draw concentric circles and see the hue sweep around each ring.
img = np.full((256, 256), 40, np.uint8)
cv2.rectangle(img, (40, 60), (150, 200), 200, -1)
cv2.line(img, (170, 20), (240, 230), 230, 4)
img = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (5, 5), 1.0)

gx = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
gy = cv2.Sobel(img, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
theta = np.mod(np.rad2deg(np.arctan2(gy, gx)), 180.0)
mag = np.sqrt(gx * gx + gy * gy)

hsv = np.zeros((*img.shape, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
hsv[..., 0] = (theta / 180.0 * 179).astype(np.uint8)
hsv[..., 1] = 255
hsv[..., 2] = (mag / (mag.max() + 1e-9) * 255).astype(np.uint8)
rgb = cv2.cvtColor(hsv, cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB)

plt.imshow(rgb)
plt.axis('off')
data.encouragement: Rotate a shape or add a line at a new angle and watch its colour shift — direction is just an angle, and here you can see it.
